title: Local slab penetration into lower mantle controls deep-focus seismicity and Changbaishan volcanism in northeast China

paper_content.abstract: Intraplate volcanism in the Changbaishan region of northeast China is underlain by a deep subduction-related earthquake cluster in the mantle transition zone, but the underlying physical connections between them remain elusive. Here we use teleseismic double-difference tomography to obtain high-resolution images of the subducting Pacific slab to provide better constraints on slab morphology and potential relationships with volcanism and deep-focus seismicity. Our results reveal a narrow slab tongue penetrating the lower mantle, flanked to the north and south by slabs stagnating in the mantle transition zone. This geometry creates a gap for sub-slab hot materials to ascend, providing a deep mantle source for Changbaishan volcanism. Additionally, the slab tongue is warped, which spatially coincides with a cluster of deep earthquakes, implying that an active deformation zone causes the clustered deep earthquakes. Our findings demonstrate that Changbaishan volcanism and deep-focus earthquakes are fundamentally controlled by the subducting slab’s dynamic morphology beneath northeast China.
paper_content.introduction:
Cenozoic volcanoes are widely distributed in northeast China1, with the active Changbaishan volcanic field (CVF) being the largest among them. The CVF is well known for its Millennium Eruption at Changbai/Paektu Mountain (AD 946-947)2,3, one of the biggest in recorded history4.

The CVF is an intraplate volcanic field located ~1500 km away from the Japan Trench and 1200 km behind the volcanic arc (Fig. 1). The subducted Pacific Plate extends beneath this region in the mantle transition zone (MTZ) out to about 120°E5. Basaltic melts originating from the CVF have ocean island basalt (OIB) affinity with an enriched (EM1) component3,6. Analysis of major and trace elements suggests that these melts are derived from small-fraction partial melting of a garnet-bearing mantle source7,8. The lithosphere beneath the CVF, as well as other Neogene volcanic fields in eastern China, has a thickness of less than 100 km9, thin enough to allow a small fraction of melting of enriched upwelling mantle without requiring particularly high source temperatures. Source mantle potential temperatures are estimated to be 1300–1400 °C10, which is similar to or slightly higher than average mantle values. Water contents of primitive magmas are variously argued to be <1 wt%7 or 1.2–1.8 wt%10, significantly lower than arc magmas. This implies a mantle source region with H2O concentrations ranging between 350 and 550 ppm10, which could correspond to a variety of mantle sources without requiring significant H2O sourced from a subducting slab11.

The formation mechanism of the CVF is currently a subject of intense debate. One widely discussed mechanism, dubbed the “big mantle wedge” (BMW) model12, proposes that mantle melting is triggered by deep dehydration of the subducting slab13 and/or upwelling of hydrous material within the mantle wedge14. However, this mechanism fails to explain why late Cenozoic volcanism (<1.5 Ma) is not widely distributed along the strike of the subduction zone, but rather concentrated in a specific region1. An alternative formation mechanism suggests that sub-slab hot materials upwell through a gap in the slab to supply magma for the Changbaishan volcano15. Recent seismic tomography studies provide for the existence of such a slab gap16,17. Nevertheless, it remains unclear how this slab gap in the MTZ is formed15,17.

In addition to the extensive intraplate volcanism and magmatism, another prominent geological feature in NE China is the occurrence of deep-focus earthquakes (300–650 km)18. Specifically, there exists an elongated cluster of deep-focus earthquakes in the MTZ ~300 km eastward from the CVF at depths ranging from 500 to 600 km (Fig. 1). The isolated nature of this cluster remains enigmatic; the potential mechanisms of deep-focus earthquake generation, including dehydration embrittlement19, transformational faulting of olivine20 and adiabatic shear instability18, are all dominantly temperature-controlled, and the thermal and chemical structure of the slab should be almost constant along-strike beneath East Asia21, so why should deep-focus earthquakes be localized here?

The spatial correlation between the CVF and deep-focus earthquakes raises the possibility that the two could be related. Zhao & Tian13 proposed that the frequent occurrence of deep-focus earthquakes near the CVF could be attributed to a locally more hydrated slab, where dehydration leads to brittle failure in the slab19 and enhanced volatile-flux melting beneath the CVF. However, based on the subduction zone thermal model in this region21, dehydration reactions of various hydrous minerals in the slab are most likely intersected at depths shallower than ~300 km22. In addition, this hypothesis contradicts the inferred presence of a metastable olivine wedge (MOW) in the core of the slab23,24, which indicates a minimal amount of water within it25. The connection between the CVF and deep-focus earthquakes, therefore, remains tenuous.

Interactions between the subducting slab and its surroundings are likely to influence the distribution of deep-focus earthquakes in the MTZ. Fukao and Obayashi26 conducted an analysis on the correlation between deep-focus earthquakes and slab morphology, suggesting that slabs stagnating in the MTZ are associated with deep-focus earthquakes limited to depths shallower than ∼620 km, while slabs penetrating into the more viscous lower mantle have events deeper than this threshold. In the Tonga subduction zone, intense seismicity has been attributed to the collision between a relic slab and the subducted Pacific slab27–29. More generally, high densities of deep-focus earthquakes are commonly observed in slab regions undergoing folding or more complex macro-scale deformation (e.g., ref. 30), and could be related to localized regions of high deviatoric stress31, otherwise sudden release of strain in the form of earthquakes would be prohibited32.

To better understand the origins of the slab gap in the MTZ and deep-focus earthquakes beneath NE China, as well as their potential links, we have constructed a high-resolution seismic velocity model for the subducting slab within and surrounding the MTZ to better characterize its morphology.
paper_content.results:
In this study, we employed the teleseismic double-difference tomography method33 to determine the mantle structure beneath northeast China (see Methods). Our final tomographic model clearly shows westward-dipping high Vp anomalies that correlate well with the relocated earthquake hypocenters and Slab 2.0 model34 (Supplementary Fig. 2), which can be interpreted as the subducting slab. Figure 2 shows cross sections of the Vp model along profiles that are nearly perpendicular to the trench. To the north (Profile A) and to the south (Profile F) of the cluster of deep-focus seismicity, the deep slab is flat and stagnant in the MTZ. Through the cluster of deep-focus seismicity (Profiles C and D), the high-velocity anomaly continues through the “660 km” discontinuity and down to ~800 km. At the margins of the cluster (Profiles B-C and D-E), there is a transition from slab penetration through “660 km” to stagnancy within the MTZ. Deep earthquakes within the MTZ primarily concentrate along Profile D. Synthetic test with a characteristic velocity model shows these features can be well-resolved (Supplementary Fig. 8).

The local penetration of the slab into the lower mantle can also be illustrated by a horizontal slice through the velocity image at a depth of 760 km, 100 km beneath the nominal “660 km” discontinuity (Fig. 3). This slice clearly depicts a high-velocity zone with the Changbaishan volcano situated around its southwestern corner and the cluster of deep seismicity (hypocenters at 500–600 km depth) aligned along its east edge (Fig. 3). Figure 4 presents a 3D iso-surface view of the imaged high-velocity anomaly. It is evident that this anomaly, interpreted as the subducting slab, extends through the “660 km” discontinuity to nearly 800 km at latitudes ranging from ~42oN to ~46oN, while remaining stagnant on both sides.
paper_content.methods:
Teleseismic double-difference tomography for the mantle structure in northeast China

The teleseismic double-difference tomography method utilizes both regional and global seismic stations to better resolve seismic velocity structures within and around seismically active source zones33,53. We assembled three sets of P-wave arrival-time data, including the selected ISC-EHB Bulletin dataset comprising ~770,000 P-wave arrival times from 3158 events occurring in proximity to the study region59, the selected China Digital Seismic Network dataset consisting of ~60,000 P-wave arrival times from 889 events, and the NorthEast China Extended SeiSmic Array (NECESSArray) dataset encompassing 11,000 P-wave arrival times from 145 events from September 2009 to August 201115. Overall, we gathered a total of 850,000 P-wave arrival times from 4192 events recorded by ~10,426 stations (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). From these absolute arrival times, a total of 3,500,000 P-wave differential arrival times are constructed with an average inter-event distance of 140 km.

The teleseismic double-difference tomography method employs a nested regional-global gridding scheme for inversion. In the target study area, the grid spacing is finer, with an interval of 1o in longitude, an interval of 1.5o in latitude, and varying intervals in depth. Within the MTZ, the grid spacing is set at 50 km in depth, which is finer than used in previously published velocity models. We utilize the LLNL_G3Dv360 as our initial global velocity model in three dimensions. The grid intervals of the global model are set to be 5o in both longitude and latitude while ranging from 55 to 225 km in depth. The checkerboard model resolution test and the model restoration test demonstrate that the model is well-resolved for depths from 160 km down to 1200 km, particularly within the MTZ (refer to Supplementary Information).

Furthermore, we also test tomographic inversions with different initial crustal models and global models, and the final tomographic models are shown to be robust (Supplementary Figs. 9, 10).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this study, P-wave arrival times from three datasets (ISC-EHB、CDSN and NECESSArray) have been compiled to
investigate the mantle structure of northeast China by using teleseismic double-difference tomography. The main finding of
this paper is that the pacific plate has been subducted into the lower mantle beneath the Changbaishan volcanic region
whereas it stagnates in the mantle transition zone nearby. This makes the link of the slab geometry and its control on deep-
focus seismicity and intraplate volcanism. The tomographic results are good and generally reliable. However,
the detailed structure of the subducting Pacific slab resolved by this study is quite similar to previous tomographic results (e.g., Tao et al.,
2018) as shown in the supplementary materials of Figures S10 and S11, which makes me consider the novelty of the
results. Furthermore, this is an over-interpretation of the seismic imaging with lack of geodynamics background. I think other
evidences are required to support the hypothesis proposed by authors.
A more detailed list of my thoughts follows below.
1. The initial regional model is formed by combing CRUST1.0 model in the crust and AK135 model in the mantle. Because
the 3D velocity model in the crust is used, it is necessary to introduce the raytracing method and provide some examples to
show the reliability of this method to accurately calculate travel times in the 3D initial model. It confused me why the anomaly
in the crust is not prominent in the tomographic model (Figure 2) when a 3D CRUST1.0 model was used as an initial model.
For teleseismic tomography, the crustal structures are generally not well constrained because the nearly vertical ray path in
the crustal depth. This means that the initial 3D velocity model in the crust is hardly modified by inversion and the inversion
model in the crust is supposed to be nearly the same as the CRUST1.0 model.
2. The global LLNL_G3Dv3 model (Simmons et al., 2012) was used as the initial model in three dimensions. I think the
inversion model and the initial LLNL_G3Dv3 model should be compared to show which part of the model is modified by
using the updated datasets and tomographic method during inversion. I am wondering why the authors not conduct
tomographic inversion using the global average 1D AK135 model as the initial model. At least this kind of tomographic
results is supposed to be exhibited to show the reliability of the used datasets and tomographic method.
3. The authors suggest that a gap exists within the mantle transition zone due to the complex geometry of the subducting
Pacific slab, which facilitate upward migration of sub-slab hot materials and cause the volcanism in the Changbaishan
region. The seismic images from tomographic studies mainly reflect the state of present mantle structure. The massive basalt
eruptions in the Changbaishan volcanic regions can be traced back to ~16 Ma (Liu et al., 2015), during which the geometry
and position of the pacific slab was significantly different from present seismic images, so other scenarios are supposed to
be examined. The Tianchi volcanism underwent a multi-stage evolution. The model proposed by the authors may be
associated with the latest volcanism. However, is there any evidence to support the existence of thermal anomaly in the
lower mantle beneath the Changbaishan volcanic region, considering that the cold subducted slabs continuously recycled
back to the core-mantle boundary beneath this region.
4. Lines 122-124. I think this idea was firstly proposed by Chen and Brudzinski (2001) through jointly analyzing results of
seismic tomography and fault plane solutions to investigate the nature of subducted lithosphere and deep earthquakes
beneath the Tonga back-arc. This paper should be properly cited.
5. Lines 236-241. Many geodynamic models were proposed to investigate the evolution and dynamics of the subducted
Pacific slab other than Wu et al (2023). A few much more influential works are not cited. For example, a recent geodynamic
modeling of Lin et al (2024) shows that the continental lithosphere in northeast China is tectonically controlled by the
subduction of Pacific slab, which plays an important role in leading to the migration of volcanism in this region since 28 Ma.
6. Lines 255-259. The slab reference frame should be defined to make the introduction of focal mechanisms of deep
earthquakes more clear.
7. Lines 292-293. Some evidences have been reported recently to support slab deformation at depths of mantle transition
zone of the northwestern Pacific subduction systems, such as Guo et al (2021) and Montagner et al (2021).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Gao et al. conducted a tomographic study on the East Asia region using the teleseismic double-difference tomography
method and discovered a slab tongue beneath the MTZ where the Pacific plate is subducting. The author suggests that the
deep earthquakes occurring in the East Asia region are related to this feature. This article is highly interesting and is sure to
attract the attention of colleagues studying the East Asia region. It is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after
major revisions. The corresponding author, Prof. Zhang, is highly reputable in the field of seismic tomography, so I have no
additional comments on the tomography methods or the robustness of the model. I have only several suggestions for the
interpretation of the model that the authors might consider to enhance the overall narrative.
1. In Figure 2, profiles C, D, and E all seem to show that there are also some remnant slabs in the MTZ above the slab
tongue, which appears more like a double-layered high-velocity anomaly. This feature is not reflected in the schematic
diagrams in Figures 4 and 5. Would this omission affect the overall framework of the story?
2. In Zhang et al.(2019, Nature Communication), a similar feature (double-layered high-velocity anomaly or slab tongue) was
observed in the Izu-Bonin region, as seen in profile A-B in Figure 2 of Zhang et al. (2019). Does this double-layered high-
velocity anomaly also represent a slab tongue similar to that in the present study? Are the deep earthquakes in the Izu-Bonin
region also related to the slab tongue? The 2015 Bonin earthquake, studied in Zhang (2019), is thought to be controlled by
slab tearing. If a slab tongue exists in the East Asia region, then slab tearing must also be present. Why are deep
earthquakes distributed along the slab tear, similar to the Izu-Bonin region, not observed in East Asia? Is the double-layered
high-velocity anomaly or slab tongue observed in the East Asia and Izu-Bonin regions generated by the same tectonic
mechanism? If the mechanisms behind the deep earthquakes in these two regions can be unified, it would have significant
implications for the universality of the model.
3. Figure 3 presents the velocity distribution at 760 km and compares it with the depth of 660 km obtained from receiver
function studies. Why not directly use the velocity distribution at 660 km for comparison? From the 760 km velocity
distribution, it seems that this slab tongue extends from 47.5 degrees to 39-38 degrees, meaning that the southern boundary
of this slab tongue should be around 38.5 degrees. Can we consider that intraplate volcanism such as Jingpohu, Longgang,
Changbaishan, and those south of 40 degrees are all controlled by this slab tongue? Why are deep earthquakes within the
38.5-40.5 degree range much fewer than those to the north?
4. The model of Tang et al. (2014) shows the slab gap. Chen et al. (2017) attributed the slab gap to an artifact of teleseismic
data. How can the authors exclude this? Is there any slab tongue found in the two tomography models?
5. What is the depth range of earthquakes affected by this slab tongue? Does it only influence earthquakes below 500 km?
Will it also affect earthquakes around 400 km?
6. Lines 55 & 57: The “NE China” and “Northeast China” should match with each other.
7. Lines 83 & 84: The water content is not the criteria to discriminate the OIB and EM1, the high water content can also
appear in EM1 mantle.
8. Lines 108-116: Very interesting. I want to remind the author that there may also be significant amounts of water and
volatiles in the subducting oceanic crust, so this model doesn't necessarily contradict the model of the metastable olivine
wedge (with low water content within the slab). I checked Line 114, and the reference 'Jing et al.' should be 'Jiang et al’.
9. Lines 231-234: I checked the article by Han et al. (2024), and they only detected localized vertical flow, which does not
directly indicate the presence of an upwelling penetrating the slab. The citation here could potentially mislead readers.
10. Lines 236-240: I didn't understand what this section is trying to convey. What is the connection between the time points
of 20 Ma and 5 Ma and the slab gap? How did you arrive at this conclusion: 'Therefore, the linkage of the slab gap in the
MTZ with the Changbaishan volcanism is also supported by the timing of volcanism and slab stagnation.'?" The Pacific slab
has started to be stagnant in the MTZ since ~20 Ma, which is earlier than the initiation of the Changbaishan volcanism
(~5Ma). So, the chronology of volcanism does not directly support the slab gap model, nor does it directly rule out the big
mantle wedge model.
11. Lines 254-258: Based on Figure 3, it doesn't seem that this pattern is apparent (In the center of the penetrating section of
the slab, most of the focal mechanisms suggest along-strike extension. At the edges of the penetrating slab, slab-normal
extension is observed).

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers
Reviewer #2:
In this study, P-wave arrival times from three datasets (ISC-EHB、CDSN and
NECESSArray) have been compiled to investigate the mantle structure of northeast
China by using teleseismic double-difference tomography. The main finding of this
paper is that the pacific plate has been subducted into the lower mantle beneath the
Changbaishan volcanic region whereas it stagnates in the mantle transition zone nearby.
This makes the link of the slab geometry and its control on deep-focus seismicity and
intraplate volcanism. The tomographic results are good and generally reliable. However,
the detailed structure of the subducting Pacific slab resolved by this study is quite
similar to previous tomographic results (e.g., Tao et al., 2018) as shown in the
supplementary materials of Figures S10 and S11, which makes me consider the novelty
of the results. Furthermore, this is an over-interpretation of the seismic imaging with
lack of geodynamics background. I think other evidences are required to support the
hypothesis proposed by authors.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your constructive comments, which are helpful for
improving our manuscript. We agree with you on the fact that our model is consistent
with main features of the FWEA18 model (Tao et al., 2018), which was determined by
the full waveform inversion. This actually proves the reliability of our velocity model,
which is determined by a different tomographic method and different datasets. However,
Tao et al. (2018) did not discuss the important slab morphology change in the MTZ and
its link with the formation of the slab gap introduced by Tang et al. (2014) and the deep
seismicity cluster to the east of the Changbaishan volcano. Actually, after Tang et al.
(2014) proposed the slab gap model responsible for the formation of the Changbaishan
volcano, it is actually questioned by some studies. For example, Lei et al. (2018)
questioned the existence of the slab gap proposed by Tang et al. (2014) (Lei, J., Zhao,
D., Xu, Y., Fan, Q., Mi, Q., Du, M., & Lu, M. (2018). Is there a gap in the stagnant
Pacific slab in the mantle transition zone under the Changbaishan volcano?. Acta
Petrologica Sinica, 34(1), 13-22). They questioned the slab gap could be an artifact
introduced by the teleseismic tomography method used by Tang et al. (2014) (Chen, C.,
Zhao, D., Tian, Y., Wu, S., Hasegawa, A., Lei, J., ... & Kang, I. B. (2017). Mantle
transition zone, stagnant slab and intraplate volcanism in Northeast Asia. Geophysical
Journal International, 209(1), 68-85). Therefore, it is still not clear what exactly caused
the formation of the CVF: big mantle wedge model or slab gap model. Through our
independent study, we actually showed the slab gap indeed exists in the MTZ.
However, Tang et al. (2014) did not provide the mechanism why there exists a slab gap
beneath the CVF. Our study for the first time proposed that the slab morphology
transition from slab stagnation to slab penetration to slab stagnation from north to south
is the cause for the formation of the slab gap. Moreover, for the first time we also link
the isolated deep seismicity cluster with this slab morphology change in the MTZ.
This also provides an outstanding example that the local slab deformation is actually the
fundamental cause for the deep-focus seismicity, a long-time outstanding geoscience
mystery to be answered. We think these new findings from our study will make great
contributions to the understanding of intraplate volcanism and deep-focus seismicity.
It is true that the full waveform inversion could provide more detailed velocity
structures. However, many studies have shown that it could also produce artifacts in
the velocity model, making it difficult to discern true or false features. As seen in the
FWEA18 model, although there are more detailed features, they are complex and
challenging for reasonable geological interpretation, and the slab morphology change
in the MTZ is not clear. In comparison, the slab morphology change and thus the slab
tearing features are very distinct in our model, which are first reported by our study.
Therefore, although our model bears some similar features to the FWEA18 model, it
does not necessarily mean that our study is not novel. We should emphasize again that
the first finding of the slab morphology change in the MTZ and its linkage to both
Changbaishan volcanism and the nearby deep seismicity cluster makes our study
unique and novel.
Based on the seismic images obtained in our study, we only interpret the slab
morphology change in the MTZ and propose it causes the slab gap in the MTZ. These
features are clear by themselves and we do not think we overinterpret them. We actually
use an existing geodynamic modeling study to explain why there exists a local slab
penetration beneath the CVF, as follows:
“The reason for localized slab penetration may also be related to slab shape. The dip
of the subducting Pacific plate undergoes a rotation from north-northwestward to west-
northwestward around 45°N, accompanied by a corresponding rotation in the
orientation of the trench, resulting in the formation of a subduction cusp (Fig. 1).
Geodynamic modeling results indicate slab penetration is favored near to this
subduction cusp where the slab dip angle is the smallest and the trench retreat velocity
is slowest (Zhao et al., 2021). Away from the cusp, the velocity of trench retreat is
higher and the slab is more likely to flatten and stagnate within the MTZ (Zhao et al.,
2021).”
We agree that it would be more supportive if a three-dimensional geodynamic modeling
could be done for east Asia to show this slab morphology change, but we think this
would need extensive work, and is beyond the scope of this study. Similar to our
previous work on Izu-Bonin that imaged slab overturn in the MTZ (Zhang et al., 2019,
NC), recently Li et al. (2024) is able to simulate this phenomenon by geodynamic
modeling (Liu et al. (2024). Slab segmentation and stacking in mantle transition zone
controls disparate surface and lower mantle subducting rates and complex slab
morphology. Geophysical Research Letters, 51(17), e2024GL110202). We hope after
our velocity images are published, some groups can also conduct geodynamic modeling
to simulate features that we imaged, which will be very useful for understanding the
dynamics in the region.
For other comments, we have made point to point responses, as follows.

Geodynamic modeling of Wu et al. (2022) has shown the Izanagi plate has been totally

“The geodynamic modelling has shown that Izanagi plate has been totally fallen into
the lower mantle since ~10-20 Ma in east Asia, which can trigger the upwelling of hot

Wu, B., Wang, Y. & Huang, J. Dynamics of the Subducted Izanagi-Pacific Plates Since the

in the Mt. Changbai volcano. Bull. Mineral. Pet. Geochem 34, 710–723 (2015).

The revised sentences are as follows:
“In the center of the penetrating section of slab (Fig. 2, Profile D), most of the focal
mechanisms suggest along-strike extension and down-dip compression (i.e., strike-slip
motion in the plane of the slab). At the edges of the penetrating slab segment (Profiles
C and E), slab-normal extension and down-dip compression is seen (i.e., thrust faulting

7. Lines 292-293. Some evidences have been reported recently to support slab
deformation at depths of mantle transition zone of the northwestern Pacific subduction
systems, such as Guo et al (2021) and Montagner et al (2021).

missed these relevant papers. Accordingly, we have revised the manuscript to include

“The region of slab penetration exhibits strong approximately NS-oriented azimuthal
anisotropy at depths of 500 and 800 km (Montagner et al., 2021) and no radial
anisotropy in the MTZ (Guo and Zhou, 2021), consistent with the orientation of
fractures formed for local slab penetration through the 660-km interface.”
Guo, Z. & Zhou, Y. Stagnant Slabs and Their Return Flows From Finite‐Frequency
Tomography of the 410‐km and 660‐km Discontinuities. JGR Solid Earth 126,
e2020JB021099 (2021).
Montagner, J.-P., Burgos, G., Capdeville, Y., Beucler, E. & Mocquet, A. The mantle

Reviewer #3:
Gao et al. conducted a tomographic study on the East Asia region using the teleseismic
double-difference tomography method and discovered a slab tongue beneath the MTZ
where the Pacific plate is subducting. The author suggests that the deep earthquakes
occurring in the East Asia region are related to this feature. This article is highly
interesting and is sure to attract the attention of colleagues studying the East Asia region.
It is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after major revisions. The
corresponding author, Prof. Zhang, is highly reputable in the field of seismic
tomography, so I have no additional comments on the tomography methods or the
robustness of the model. I have only several suggestions for the interpretation of the
model that the authors might consider to enhance the overall narrative.
Response: Thanks for encouraging and constructive comments, which help us to
improve our manuscript. We hope the revised manuscript has better clarified some
unclear issues raised by you.
1. In Figure 2, profiles C, D, and E all seem to show that there are also some remnant
slabs in the MTZ above the slab tongue, which appears more like a double-layered high-
velocity anomaly. This feature is not reflected in the schematic diagrams in Figures 4
and 5. Would this omission affect the overall framework of the story?
Response: Thanks for catching this interesting feature for us. By the checkerboard and
characteristic model tests, the region that this feature appears is relatively well resolved.
Not including it in the diagram would not affect the story presented in this study. Again
for the fully understanding this phenomenon would need complex geodynamic
modelling. We have included some discussions on this feature and its connection with
the Izu-Bonin slab feature in the revised manuscript, as follows:
“One interesting feature of our tomographic images along Profiles C and D is that the
high velocity anomaly bifurcates at around 600 km depth, with a 300-500 km long high
velocity “limb” lying flat along the “660 km” discontinuity, and a longer “limb”
penetrating into the lower mantle. This feature appears to be well-resolved (see
Supplementary Materials). Given the high viscosity of subducting slabs, we feel that
this is unlikely to be “splitting” of the slab, and may instead represent one contiguous
slab and a stranded slab fragment. This feature could represent the footprint of the slab
morphology change from slab stagnation within and penetration through the MTZ. This
high velocity bifurcation differs from the features we observed in the Izu-Bonin
subduction zone, where some high velocity anomalies are observed in the uppermost
lower mantle. Those anomalies probably represent slow sinking of “stagnant” slab
materials through the 660 km interface, which is not a perfect barrier to convection
(Čížková & Bina, 2019).”
2.
2.1 In Zhang et al.(2019, Nature Communication), a similar feature (double-layered
high-velocity anomaly or slab tongue) was observed in the Izu-Bonin region, as seen in
profile A-B in Figure 2 of Zhang et al. (2019). Does this double-layered high-
velocity anomaly also represent a slab tongue similar to that in the present study?
Are the deep earthquakes in the Izu-Bonin region also related to the slab tongue?
Response: Thanks for also mentioning high-velocity anomaly beneath the flat-lying
slab along the profiles a and b in the Izu-Bonin region in our previous study (Zhang et
al., 2019). The feature seen in Zhang et al. (2019) is different from the one in the present
study. The high-velocity anomaly beneath the flat-lying slab in the Izu-Bonin region
represents part of stagnant slab materials being slowly penetrated through the 660 km
discontinuity. We have revised the text accordingly:
“This high velocity bifurcation differs from the features we observed in the Izu-Bonin
subduction zone, where some high velocity anomalies are observed in the uppermost
lower mantle. Those anomalies probably represent slow sinking of “stagnant” slab
materials through the 660 km interface, which is not a perfect barrier to convection
(Čížková & Bina, 2019).”
2.2 The 2015 Bonin earthquake, studied in Zhang (2019), is thought to be controlled by
slab tearing. If a slab tongue exists in the East Asia region, then slab tearing must also
be present. Why are deep earthquakes distributed along the slab tear, similar to the Izu-
Bonin region, not observed in East Asia? Is the double-layered high-velocity anomaly
or slab tongue observed in the East Asia and Izu-Bonin regions generated by the same
tectonic mechanism? If the mechanisms behind the deep earthquakes in these two
regions can be unified, it would have significant implications for the universality of the
model.
Response: Zhang et al. (2019) found that the 2015 Bonin earthquake occurred “<30 km
south of the tear in the slab, near the fold hinge where the slab rotates from near-vertical
to overturned”. Therefore, the 2015 M7.9 earthquake did not occur along the slab tear,
but some distance away near the fold hinge, where the strain is supposed to be large.
We agree with you that slab tearing should also occur when the slab morphology
changes in the MTZ. As seen in Figure 4, deep seismicity did not occur along the slab
tears, but along the warping region of the slab tongue where the deformation is the
greatest. In this sense, the mechanisms producing deep seismicity in both regions are
similar, which are controlled by local slab deformation. The reason that the deep
seismicity did occur along slab tear is most likely because it is too hot to have brittle
deformation. We have reenforced this argument in the revised manuscript, as follows:
“It is noted that deep seismicity clustering is only seen along the warping region of the
slab tongue, and not along slab tears created when slab transits from stagnation above
to penetration through the 660 km discontinuity and then reverses. This is also the case
observed in the Izu-Bonin subduction zone (Zhang et al., 2019). This may be because
shear heating and conductive heating near to the slab tears render temperatures too
high for brittle deformation to occur.”
3. Figure 3 presents the velocity distribution at 760 km and compares it with the depth
of 660 km obtained from receiver function studies. Why not directly use the velocity
distribution at 660 km for comparison? From the 760 km velocity distribution, it seems
that this slab tongue extends from 47.5 degrees to 39-38 degrees, meaning that the
southern boundary of this slab tongue should be around 38.5 degrees. Can we consider
that intraplate volcanism such as Jingpohu, Longgang, Changbaishan, and those south
of 40 degrees are all controlled by this slab tongue? Why are deep earthquakes within
the 38.5-40.5 degree range much fewer than those to the north?
Response: For comparison the local slab penetration region with the 660 km
discontinuity depression region imaged by receiver functions, it is better to use the 760-
km velocity depth slice than the 660 km slice. In this way, because slabs are stagnant
in the MTZ outside the slab penetration region, the velocity in the 760 km depth beneath
the slab penetration region should be higher, as shown in Figure 3. For the slab
penetration region through the 660 km discontinuity, the interface should be depressed.
The fact that the depressed region is in accordance with the area where the slab
penetrated through the 660-km discontinuity supports the reliability of our velocity
model.
In Figure 3, the blue rectangle indicates an estimate of the main slab penetrated region
at a depth of 760 km, which extends from 46.3 degrees to 42 degrees in latitude. The
reason that within the 38.5-40.5 degree range there are much fewer deep earthquakes
than those to the north is likely because the local strain rates induced by slab
deformation are smaller in this region that is farther away from the main slab
penetration area.
Based on the spatial correlation between the slab penetration region and volcanoes of
Jingpohu, Longgang, Changbaishan, and those south of 40 degrees, we think the
intraplate volcanism in this region is partly controlled by this slab tongue. We have
made this point clear in the manuscript.
“Additionally, our findings indicate that other nearby volcanoes such as Jingpohu
and Longgang are also situated around this same slab gap, suggesting a shared origin
(Figs. 3-5).”
4. The model of Tang et al. (2014) shows the slab gap. Chen et al. (2017) attributed the
slab gap to an artifact of teleseismic data. How can the authors exclude this? Is there
any slab tongue found in the two tomography models?
Response: We should emphasize that the teleseismic tomography method used in our
study is totally different from that illustrated in Chen et al. (2017). The teleseismic
double-difference tomography method adopted in our study uses differential times from
regional events recorded by global seismic stations, instead of travel times from
teleseismic events recorded by regional stations. In addition, we did not use relative
travel time residuals determined by subtracting average delay times in the study region.
Therefore, our teleseismic tomography method will not create artifacts shown in Chen
et al. (2017). Actually, the tomography method used in Tang et al. (2014) is also
different from that in Chen et al. (2017). Tang et al. (2014) used finite-frequency
tomography method, which employs Born-Fréchet kernels to account for effects of off-
raypath structures on traveltime data. The data they used in the inversion are differential
travel times between station pairs which are measured by a cross-correlation based
method. Consequently, both the data processing procedure and the tomography method
used by Tang et al. (2014) are different from those applied by Chen et al. (2017).
Moreover, two independent seismic tomography studies, Tao et al. (2018) and Ma et al.
(2018), also vaguely imaged the local slab penetration into the lower mantle, consistent
with our velocity images. As a consequence, the slab gap or slab tongue for the
subducting Pacific plate is real beneath the CVF. We have made this point clearer in
the Supplementary Materials, as follows:
“For the inversion, we use the multiscale teleseismic double-difference (DD)
tomography method of Pesicek et al. (2014), which is a global version of the DD seismic
tomography method (tomoDD) (Zhang and Thurber, 2003, 2006). It utilizes the pseudo-
bending raytracing algorithm (Um and Thurber, 1987) to determine the ray paths and
compute the travel times between events and stations within a spherical Earth model.
The pseudo-bending raytracing method is very efficient and has been widely used in
seismic tomography studies at various scales (e.g., Zhao et al., 1992; Chiarabba et al.,
2000; Rawlingson et al., 2010).
Compared to the conventional teleseismic tomography method, as described in Chen et
al. (2017), the teleseismic DD tomography method uses both absolute event-station
arrival times and differential arrival times from pairs of regional events observed on
global seismic stations to simultaneously determine event locations and seismic velocity
models. This is in contrast to the conventional teleseismic tomography method that uses
arrival times from teleseismic events recorded on regional seismic stations to determine
velocity structure beneath stations. As a result, teleseismic DD tomography method is
not subject to potential artifacts introduced by conventional teleseismic tomography
described in Chen et al. (2017).”
5. What is the depth range of earthquakes affected by this slab tongue? Does it only
influence earthquakes below 500 km? Will it also affect earthquakes around 400 km?
Response: The depth range of earthquakes affected by this slab tongue depends on the
distribution of high strain rates induced by local slab deformation related to the slab
morphology change in the MTZ. Based on cross sections of seismicity shown in Figure
1 and Figure S14, the slab tongue mainly affects earthquakes deeper than ~400 km. We
have added one sentence in the revised manuscript to state this fact, as follows:
“From cross sections of seismicity shown in Figure 1 and Figure S14, the local slab
penetration beneath the CVF mainly affects the seismicity deeper than ~400 km based
on the fact that the slab seismicity is distributed above ~400 km outside the slab
penetration region.”
6. Lines 55 & 57: The “NE China” and “Northeast China” should match with each other.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. The relevant sentences have been corrected.
7. Lines 83 & 84: The water content is not the criteria to discriminate the OIB and EM1,
the high water content can also appear in EM1 mantle.
Response: Thanks for pointing this out. We have revised this sentence accordingly:
“This implies a mantle source region with H O concentrations ranging between 350-
2
550 ppm (Kuritani et al., 2019), which could correspond to a variety of mantle sources
without requiring significant H O sourced from a subducting slab (Jamtveit et al.,
2
2001).”
8. Lines 108-116: Very interesting. I want to remind the author that there may also be
significant amounts of water and volatiles in the subducting oceanic crust, so this model
doesn't necessarily contradict the model of the metastable olivine wedge (with low
water content within the slab). I checked Line 114, and the reference 'Jing et al.' should
be 'Jiang et al’.
Response: Based on the thermal model for the Pacific plate subduction in east Asia,
dehydration reactions of various hydrous minerals in the subducting oceanic crust and
mantle would have been finished at depth of ~300 km (Hacker et al., 2003). This is the
reason why we think this is a contradiction. We have slightly revised the text to make
this point clearer.
“However, based on the subduction zone thermal model in this region (Syracuse et al.,
2010), dehydration reactions of various hydrous minerals in the slab are most likely
intersected at depths shallower than ~300 km (Hacker et al., 2003). In addition, this
hypothesis contradicts the inferred presence of a metastable olivine wedge (MOW) in
the core of the slab (Jiang et al., 2008; Shen and Zhan, 2020), which indicates a
minimal amount of water within it (Green et al., 2010).”
The typo “'Jing et al.'” has been changed to “Jiang et al.”
9. Lines 231-234: I checked the article by Han et al. (2024), and they only detected
localized vertical flow, which does not directly indicate the presence of an upwelling
penetrating the slab. The citation here could potentially mislead readers.
Response: Sorry for not making this point clear. If there exists a slab gap and hot mantle
materials from lower mantle upwell through this gap, the upwelling “plume” should be
localized above the slab gap, instead of widespread in the big mantle wedge. Seismic
anisotropy study of Han et al. (2024) found localized vertical flow, consistent with the
existence of the slab gap and its role on forming the CVF. We have slightly revised the
manuscript to make this point clearer, as follows:
“Recent seismic anisotropy analysis further supports the idea of mantle flow migrating
upwards through the slab by revealing a localized region of vertical flow directly
beneath Changbaishan volcano (Han et al., 2024).”
10. Lines 236-240: I didn't understand what this section is trying to convey. What is the
connection between the time points of 20 Ma and 5 Ma and the slab gap? How did you
arrive at this conclusion: 'Therefore, the linkage of the slab gap in the MTZ with the
Changbaishan volcanism is also supported by the timing of volcanism and slab
stagnation.'?" The Pacific slab has started to be stagnant in the MTZ since ~20 Ma,
which is earlier than the initiation of the Changbaishan volcanism (~5Ma). So, the
chronology of volcanism does not directly support the slab gap model, nor does it
directly rule out the big mantle wedge model.
Response: Following the suggestion of reviewer #2, we have included a recent
geodynamic modelling of Lin et al. (2024) in the revised manuscript. As a result, we
have revised the part accordingly to make the argument more logic.
“It is important to recognize that the length and position of the Pacific slab, and
volcanic activity in the CVF have changed through time. The Pacific slab probably only
reached the MTZ at ~20 Ma (Wu et al., 2022) or ~15 Ma (Lin et al., 2024). The earliest
massive basalt eruptions in the CVF can be traced back to ~16 Ma (Liu et al., 2015b),
probably predating the presence of a stagnant slab (Lin et al., 2024). At ~15 Ma, the
Pacific slab started to stagnate in the MTZ and the sub-horizontal slab continued to
advance westward (Lin et al., 2024). We propose that the formation of the slab gap and
associated mantle upwelling may be associated with the shield forming stage of CVF
volcanism from ~5-1 Ma (Liu et al., 2015b; Ward et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018). We
note that this interpretation is not mutually exclusive of other mechanisms of mantle
upwelling, such as lithospheric dripping beneath the Songliao Basin (Lin et al., 2024).”
11. Lines 254-258: Based on Figure 3, it doesn't seem that this pattern is apparent (In
the center of the penetrating section of the slab, most of the focal mechanisms suggest
along-strike extension. At the edges of the penetrating slab, slab-normal extension is
observed).
Response: We acknowledge that the distribution of focal mechanisms is not very clear
due to the overlapping of different types of mechanisms on Figure 3. To clarify, we
have revised Supplementary Figure 15 to also plot the histogram of normal fault, thrust
fault and strike-slip fault mechanisms along latitude. The related text is as follows:
“Focal mechanisms from the Global Centroid Moment tensor catalog indicate down-
dip compression and a mixture of slab-normal and along-strike extension (Gan et al.,
2015; Supplementary Figure 15). In the center of the penetrating section of slab (Fig.
2, Profile D), most of the focal mechanisms suggest along-strike extension and down-
dip compression (i.e., strike-slip motion in the plane of the slab). At the edges of the
penetrating slab segment (Profiles C and E), slab-normal extension and down-dip
compression is seen (i.e., thrust faulting in the plane of the slab), similar to shallower
events (Zhao and Ohtani, 2009; Gan et al., 2015).”
Supplementary Figure 15 Distribution of deep-focus earthquakes and their focal mechanisms in the
mantle transition zone in northeast China. (a) Map view of deep-focus earthquakes, denoted as
beachballs with colors representing the source depth. Each earthquake is indexed with the first letter
T representing thrust-fault focal mechanism, N representing normal-fault focal mechanism, and S
representing strike-fault focal mechanism, respectively. Slab penetration region is marked a blue

latitude.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Intraplate volcanism in the Changbaishan region of northeast China is underlain by a deep subduction-related earthquake cluster in the mantle transition zone, but the underlying physical connections between them remain elusive. Here we use teleseismic double-difference tomography to obtain high-resolution images of the subducting Pacific slab to provide better constraints on slab morphology and potential relationships with volcanism and deep-focus seismicity. Our results reveal a narrow slab tongue penetrating the lower mantle, flanked to the north and south by slabs stagnating in the mantle transition zone. This geometry creates a gap for sub-slab hot materials to ascend, providing a deep mantle source for Changbaishan volcanism. Additionally, the slab tongue is warped, which spatially coincides with a cluster of deep earthquakes, implying that an active deformation zone causes the clustered deep earthquakes. Our findings demonstrate that Changbaishan volcanism and deep-focus earthquakes are fundamentally controlled by the subducting slab’s dynamic morphology beneath northeast China.

---

## Introduction

Cenozoic volcanoes are widely distributed in northeast China1, with the active Changbaishan volcanic field (CVF) being the largest among them. The CVF is well known for its Millennium Eruption at Changbai/Paektu Mountain (AD 946-947)2,3, one of the biggest in recorded history4.

The CVF is an intraplate volcanic field located ~1500 km away from the Japan Trench and 1200 km behind the volcanic arc (Fig. 1). The subducted Pacific Plate extends beneath this region in the mantle transition zone (MTZ) out to about 120°E5. Basaltic melts originating from the CVF have ocean island basalt (OIB) affinity with an enriched (EM1) component3,6. Analysis of major and trace elements suggests that these melts are derived from small-fraction partial melting of a garnet-bearing mantle source7,8. The lithosphere beneath the CVF, as well as other Neogene volcanic fields in eastern China, has a thickness of less than 100 km9, thin enough to allow a small fraction of melting of enriched upwelling mantle without requiring particularly high source temperatures. Source mantle potential temperatures are estimated to be 1300–1400 °C10, which is similar to or slightly higher than average mantle values. Water contents of primitive magmas are variously argued to be <1 wt%7 or 1.2–1.8 wt%10, significantly lower than arc magmas. This implies a mantle source region with H2O concentrations ranging between 350 and 550 ppm10, which could correspond to a variety of mantle sources without requiring significant H2O sourced from a subducting slab11.

The formation mechanism of the CVF is currently a subject of intense debate. One widely discussed mechanism, dubbed the “big mantle wedge” (BMW) model12, proposes that mantle melting is triggered by deep dehydration of the subducting slab13 and/or upwelling of hydrous material within the mantle wedge14. However, this mechanism fails to explain why late Cenozoic volcanism (<1.5 Ma) is not widely distributed along the strike of the subduction zone, but rather concentrated in a specific region1. An alternative formation mechanism suggests that sub-slab hot materials upwell through a gap in the slab to supply magma for the Changbaishan volcano15. Recent seismic tomography studies provide for the existence of such a slab gap16,17. Nevertheless, it remains unclear how this slab gap in the MTZ is formed15,17.

In addition to the extensive intraplate volcanism and magmatism, another prominent geological feature in NE China is the occurrence of deep-focus earthquakes (300–650 km)18. Specifically, there exists an elongated cluster of deep-focus earthquakes in the MTZ ~300 km eastward from the CVF at depths ranging from 500 to 600 km (Fig. 1). The isolated nature of this cluster remains enigmatic; the potential mechanisms of deep-focus earthquake generation, including dehydration embrittlement19, transformational faulting of olivine20 and adiabatic shear instability18, are all dominantly temperature-controlled, and the thermal and chemical structure of the slab should be almost constant along-strike beneath East Asia21, so why should deep-focus earthquakes be localized here?

The spatial correlation between the CVF and deep-focus earthquakes raises the possibility that the two could be related. Zhao & Tian13 proposed that the frequent occurrence of deep-focus earthquakes near the CVF could be attributed to a locally more hydrated slab, where dehydration leads to brittle failure in the slab19 and enhanced volatile-flux melting beneath the CVF. However, based on the subduction zone thermal model in this region21, dehydration reactions of various hydrous minerals in the slab are most likely intersected at depths shallower than ~300 km22. In addition, this hypothesis contradicts the inferred presence of a metastable olivine wedge (MOW) in the core of the slab23,24, which indicates a minimal amount of water within it25. The connection between the CVF and deep-focus earthquakes, therefore, remains tenuous.

Interactions between the subducting slab and its surroundings are likely to influence the distribution of deep-focus earthquakes in the MTZ. Fukao and Obayashi26 conducted an analysis on the correlation between deep-focus earthquakes and slab morphology, suggesting that slabs stagnating in the MTZ are associated with deep-focus earthquakes limited to depths shallower than ∼620 km, while slabs penetrating into the more viscous lower mantle have events deeper than this threshold. In the Tonga subduction zone, intense seismicity has been attributed to the collision between a relic slab and the subducted Pacific slab27–29. Response to Reviewers
Reviewer #2:
In this study, P-wave arrival times from three datasets (ISC-EHB、CDSN and
NECESSArray) have been compiled to investigate the mantle structure of northeast
China by using teleseismic double-difference tomography. The main finding of this
paper is that the pacific plate has been subducted into the lower mantle beneath the
Changbaishan volcanic region whereas it stagnates in the mantle transition zone nearby.
This makes the link of the slab geometry and its control on deep-focus seismicity and
intraplate volcanism. The tomographic results are good and generally reliable. However,
the detailed structure of the subducting Pacific slab resolved by this study is quite
similar to previous tomographic results (e.g., Tao et al., 2018) as shown in the
supplementary materials of Figures S10 and S11, which makes me consider the novelty
of the results. Furthermore, this is an over-interpretation of the seismic imaging with

Response: We sincerely appreciate your constructive comments, which are helpful for
improving our manuscript. We agree with you on the fact that our model is consistent
with main features of the FWEA18 model (Tao et al., 2018), which was determined by
the full waveform inversion. This actually proves the reliability of our velocity model,
which is determined by a different tomographic method and different datasets. However,
Tao et al. (2018) did not discuss the important slab morphology change in the MTZ and
its link with the formation of the slab gap introduced by Tang et al. (2014) and the deep
seismicity cluster to the east of the Changbaishan volcano. Actually, after Tang et al.
(2014) proposed the slab gap model responsible for the formation of the Changbaishan
volcano, it is actually questioned by some studies. For example, Lei et al. (2018)
questioned the existence of the slab gap proposed by Tang et al. (2014) (Lei, J., Zhao,
D., Xu, Y., Fan, Q., Mi, Q., Du, M., & Lu, M. (2018). Is there a gap in the stagnant
Pacific slab in the mantle transition zone under the Changbaishan volcano?. Acta
Petrologica Sinica, 34(1), 13-22). They questioned the slab gap could be an artifact
introduced by the teleseismic tomography method used by Tang et al. (2014) (Chen, C.,
Zhao, D., Tian, Y., Wu, S., Hasegawa, A., Lei, J., ... & Kang, I. B. (2017). Mantle
transition zone, stagnant slab and intraplate volcanism in Northeast Asia. Geophysical
Journal International, 209(1), 68-85). Therefore, it is still not clear what exactly caused
the formation of the CVF: big mantle wedge model or slab gap model. Through our
independent study, we actually showed the slab gap indeed exists in the MTZ.
However, Tang et al. (2014) did not provide the mechanism why there exists a slab gap
beneath the CVF. Our study for the first time proposed that the slab morphology
transition from slab stagnation to slab penetration to slab stagnation from north to south
is the cause for the formation of the slab gap. Moreover, for the first time we also link
the isolated deep seismicity cluster with this slab morphology change in the MTZ.
This also provides an outstanding example that the local slab deformation is actually the
fundamental cause for the deep-focus seismicity, a long-time outstanding geoscience
mystery to be answered. We think these new findings from our study will make great
contributions to the understanding of intraplate volcanism and deep-focus seismicity.
It is true that the full waveform inversion could provide more detailed velocity
structures. However, many studies have shown that it could also produce artifacts in
the velocity model, making it difficult to discern true or false features. As seen in the
FWEA18 model, although there are more detailed features, they are complex and
challenging for reasonable geological interpretation, and the slab morphology change
in the MTZ is not clear. In comparison, the slab morphology change and thus the slab
tearing features are very distinct in our model, which are first reported by our study.
Therefore, although our model bears some similar features to the FWEA18 model, it
does not necessarily mean that our study is not novel. We should emphasize again that
the first finding of the slab morphology change in the MTZ and its linkage to both
Changbaishan volcanism and the nearby deep seismicity cluster makes our study
unique and novel.
Based on the seismic images obtained in our study, we only interpret the slab
morphology change in the MTZ and propose it causes the slab gap in the MTZ. These
features are clear by themselves and we do not think we overinterpret them. We actually
use an existing geodynamic modeling study to explain why there exists a local slab
penetration beneath the CVF, as follows:
“The reason for localized slab penetration may also be related to slab shape. The dip
of the subducting Pacific plate undergoes a rotation from north-northwestward to west-
northwestward around 45°N, accompanied by a corresponding rotation in the
orientation of the trench, resulting in the formation of a subduction cusp (Fig. 1).
Geodynamic modeling results indicate slab penetration is favored near to this
subduction cusp where the slab dip angle is the smallest and the trench retreat velocity
is slowest (Zhao et al., 2021). Away from the cusp, the velocity of trench retreat is
higher and the slab is more likely to flatten and stagnate within the MTZ (Zhao et al.,
2021).”
We agree that it would be more supportive if a three-dimensional geodynamic modeling
could be done for east Asia to show this slab morphology change, but we think this
would need extensive work, and is beyond the scope of this study. Similar to our
previous work on Izu-Bonin that imaged slab overturn in the MTZ (Zhang et al., 2019,
NC), recently Li et al. (2024) is able to simulate this phenomenon by geodynamic
modeling (Liu et al. (2024). Slab segmentation and stacking in mantle transition zone
controls disparate surface and lower mantle subducting rates and complex slab
morphology. Geophysical Research Letters, 51(17), e2024GL110202). We hope after
our velocity images are published, some groups can also conduct geodynamic modeling
to simulate features that we imaged, which will be very useful for understanding the
dynamics in the region.

regional events recorded by global seismic stations, instead of travel times from
teleseismic events recorded by regional stations. In addition, we did not use relative

Therefore, our teleseismic tomography method will not create artifacts shown in Chen

travel times between station pairs which are measured by a cross-correlation based
method. Consequently, both the data processing procedure and the tomography method
used by Tang et al. (2014) are different from those applied by Chen et al. (2017).
Moreover, two independent seismic tomography studies, Tao et al. (2018) and Ma et al.
(2018), also vaguely imaged the local slab penetration into the lower mantle, consistent
with our velocity images. As a consequence, the slab gap or slab tongue for the
subducting Pacific plate is real beneath the CVF. We have made this point clearer in
the Supplementary Materials, as follows:

bending raytracing algorithm (Um and Thurber, 1987) to determine the ray paths and
compute the travel times between events and stations within a spherical Earth model.

seismic tomography studies at various scales (e.g., Zhao et al., 1992; Chiarabba et al.,

## Paper

## Abstract

Intraplate volcanism in the Changbaishan region of northeast China is underlain by a deep subduction-related earthquake cluster in the mantle transition zone, but the underlying physical connections between them remain elusive. Here we use teleseismic double-difference tomography to obtain high-resolution images of the subducting Pacific slab to provide better constraints on slab morphology and potential relationships with volcanism and deep-focus seismicity. Our results reveal a narrow slab tongue penetrating the lower mantle, flanked to the north and south by slabs stagnating in the mantle transition zone. This geometry creates a gap for sub-slab hot materials to ascend, providing a deep mantle source for Changbaishan volcanism. Additionally, the slab tongue is warped, which spatially coincides with a cluster of deep earthquakes, implying that an active deformation zone causes the clustered deep earthquakes. Our findings demonstrate that Changbaishan volcanism and deep-focus earthquakes are fundamentally controlled by the subducting slab’s dynamic morphology beneath northeast China.

---

## Introduction

Cenozoic volcanoes are widely distributed in northeast China1, with the active Changbaishan volcanic field (CVF) being the largest among them. The CVF is well known for its Millennium Eruption at Changbai/Paektu Mountain (AD 946-947)2,3, one of the biggest in recorded history4.

The CVF is an intraplate volcanic field located ~1500 km away from the Japan Trench and 1200 km behind the volcanic arc (Fig. 1). The subducted Pacific Plate extends beneath this region in the mantle transition zone (MTZ) out to about 120°E5. Basaltic melts originating from the CVF have ocean island basalt (OIB) affinity with an enriched (EM1) component3,6. Analysis of major and trace elements suggests that these melts are derived from small-fraction partial melting of a garnet-bearing mantle source7,8. The lithosphere beneath the CVF, as well as other Neogene volcanic fields in eastern China, has a thickness of less than 100 km9, thin enough to allow a small fraction of melting of enriched upwelling mantle without requiring particularly high source temperatures. Source mantle potential temperatures are estimated to be 1300–1400 °C10, which is similar to or slightly higher than average mantle values. Water contents of primitive magmas are variously argued to be <1 wt%7 or 1.2–1.8 wt%10, significantly lower than arc magmas. This implies a mantle source region with H2O concentrations ranging between 350 and 550 ppm10, which could correspond to a variety of mantle sources without requiring significant H2O sourced from a subducting slab11.

The formation mechanism of the CVF is currently a subject of intense debate. One widely discussed mechanism, dubbed the “big mantle wedge” (BMW) model12, proposes that mantle melting is triggered by deep dehydration of the subducting slab13 and/or upwelling of hydrous material within the mantle wedge14. However, this mechanism fails to explain why late Cenozoic volcanism (<1.5 Ma) is not widely distributed along the strike of the subduction zone, but rather concentrated in a specific region1. An alternative formation mechanism suggests that sub-slab hot materials upwell through a gap in the slab to supply magma for the Changbaishan volcano15. Recent seismic tomography studies provide for the existence of such a slab gap16,17. Nevertheless, it remains unclear how this slab gap in the MTZ is formed15,17.

In addition to the extensive intraplate volcanism and magmatism, another prominent geological feature in NE China is the occurrence of deep-focus earthquakes (300–650 km)18. Specifically, there exists an elongated cluster of deep-focus earthquakes in the MTZ ~300 km eastward from the CVF at depths ranging from 500 to 600 km (Fig. 1). The isolated nature of this cluster remains enigmatic; the potential mechanisms of deep-focus earthquake generation, including dehydration embrittlement19, transformational faulting of olivine20 and adiabatic shear instability18, are all dominantly temperature-controlled, and the thermal and chemical structure of the slab should be almost constant along-strike beneath East Asia21, so why should deep-focus earthquakes be localized here?

The spatial correlation between the CVF and deep-focus earthquakes raises the possibility that the two could be related. Zhao & Tian13 proposed that the frequent occurrence of deep-focus earthquakes near the CVF could be attributed to a locally more hydrated slab, where dehydration leads to brittle failure in the slab19 and enhanced volatile-flux melting beneath the CVF. However, based on the subduction zone thermal model in this region21, dehydration reactions of various hydrous minerals in the slab are most likely intersected at depths shallower than ~300 km22. In addition, this hypothesis contradicts the inferred presence of a metastable olivine wedge (MOW) in the core of the slab23,24, which indicates a minimal amount of water within it25. The connection between the CVF and deep-focus earthquakes, therefore, remains tenuous.

Interactions between the subducting slab and its surroundings are likely to influence the distribution of deep-focus earthquakes in the MTZ. Fukao and Obayashi26 conducted an analysis on the correlation between deep-focus earthquakes and slab morphology, suggesting that slabs stagnating in the MTZ are associated with deep-focus earthquakes limited to depths shallower than ∼620 km, while slabs penetrating into the more viscous lower mantle have events deeper than this threshold. In the Tonga subduction zone, intense seismicity has been attributed to the collision between a relic slab and the subducted Pacific slab27–29. More generally, high densities of deep-focus earthquakes are commonly observed in slab regions undergoing folding or more complex macro-scale deformation (e.g., ref. 30), and could be related to localized regions of high deviatoric stress31, otherwise sudden release of strain in the form of earthquakes would be prohibited32.

To better understand the origins of the slab gap in the MTZ and deep-focus earthquakes beneath NE China, as well as their potential links, we have constructed a high-resolution seismic velocity model for the subducting slab within and surrounding the MTZ to better characterize its morphology.

---

## Results

In this study, we employed the teleseismic double-difference tomography method33 to determine the mantle structure beneath northeast China (see Methods). Our final tomographic model clearly shows westward-dipping high Vp anomalies that correlate well with the relocated earthquake hypocenters and Slab 2.0 model34 (Supplementary Fig. 2), which can be interpreted as the subducting slab. Figure 2 shows cross sections of the Vp model along profiles that are nearly perpendicular to the trench. To the north (Profile A) and to the south (Profile F) of the cluster of deep-focus seismicity, the deep slab is flat and stagnant in the MTZ. Through the cluster of deep-focus seismicity (Profiles C and D), the high-velocity anomaly continues through the “660 km” discontinuity and down to ~800 km. At the margins of the cluster (Profiles B-C and D-E), there is a transition from slab penetration through “660 km” to stagnancy within the MTZ. Deep earthquakes within the MTZ primarily concentrate along Profile D. Synthetic test with a characteristic velocity model shows these features can be well-resolved (Supplementary Fig. 8).

The local penetration of the slab into the lower mantle can also be illustrated by a horizontal slice through the velocity image at a depth of 760 km, 100 km beneath the nominal “660 km” discontinuity (Fig. 3). This slice clearly depicts a high-velocity zone with the Changbaishan volcano situated around its southwestern corner and the cluster of deep seismicity (hypocenters at 500–600 km depth) aligned along its east edge (Fig. 3). Figure 4 presents a 3D iso-surface view of the imaged high-velocity anomaly. It is evident that this anomaly, interpreted as the subducting slab, extends through the “660 km” discontinuity to nearly 800 km at latitudes ranging from ~42oN to ~46oN, while remaining stagnant on both sides.

---

## Methods

Teleseismic double-difference tomography for the mantle structure in northeast China

The teleseismic double-difference tomography method utilizes both regional and global seismic stations to better resolve seismic velocity structures within and around seismically active source zones33,53. We assembled three sets of P-wave arrival-time data, including the selected ISC-EHB Bulletin dataset comprising ~770,000 P-wave arrival times from 3158 events occurring in proximity to the study region59, the selected China Digital Seismic Network dataset consisting of ~60,000 P-wave arrival times from 889 events, and the NorthEast China Extended SeiSmic Array (NECESSArray) dataset encompassing 11,000 P-wave arrival times from 145 events from September 2009 to August 201115. Overall, we gathered a total of 850,000 P-wave arrival times from 4192 events recorded by ~10,426 stations (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). From these absolute arrival times, a total of 3,500,000 P-wave differential arrival times are constructed with an average inter-event distance of 140 km.

The teleseismic double-difference tomography method employs a nested regional-global gridding scheme for inversion. In the target study area, the grid spacing is finer, with an interval of 1o in longitude, an interval of 1.5o in latitude, and varying intervals in depth. Within the MTZ, the grid spacing is set at 50 km in depth, which is finer than used in previously published velocity models. We utilize the LLNL_G3Dv360 as our initial global velocity model in three dimensions. The grid intervals of the global model are set to be 5o in both longitude and latitude while ranging from 55 to 225 km in depth. The checkerboard model resolution test and the model restoration test demonstrate that the model is well-resolved for depths from 160 km down to 1200 km, particularly within the MTZ (refer to Supplementary Information).

Furthermore, we also test tomographic inversions with different initial crustal models and global models, and the final tomographic models are shown to be robust (Supplementary Figs. 9, 10).

seismicity cluster to the east of the Changbaishan volcano. Actually, after Tang et al.
(2014) proposed the slab gap model responsible for the formation of the Changbaishan
volcano, it is actually questioned by some studies. For example, Lei et al. (2018)
questioned the existence of the slab gap proposed by Tang et al. (2014) (Lei, J., Zhao,

transition zone, stagnant slab and intraplate volcanism in Northeast Asia. Geophysical

independent study, we actually showed the slab gap indeed exists in the MTZ.

beneath the CVF. Our study for the first time proposed that the slab morphology
transition from slab stagnation to slab penetration to slab stagnation from north to south
is the cause for the formation of the slab gap. Moreover, for the first time we also link
the isolated deep seismicity cluster with this slab morphology change in the MTZ.
This also provides an outstanding example that the local slab deformation is actually the
fundamental cause for the deep-focus seismicity, a long-time outstanding geoscience
mystery to be answered. We think these new findings from our study will make great
contributions to the understanding of intraplate volcanism and deep-focus seismicity.
It is true that the full waveform inversion could provide more detailed velocity
structures. However, many studies have shown that it could also produce artifacts in
the velocity model, making it difficult to discern true or false features. As seen in the
FWEA18 model, although there are more detailed features, they are complex and
challenging for reasonable geological interpretation, and the slab morphology change

tearing features are very distinct in our model, which are first reported by our study.

does not necessarily mean that our study is not novel. We should emphasize again that

Changbaishan volcanism and the nearby deep seismicity cluster makes our study
unique and novel.

morphology change in the MTZ and propose it causes the slab gap in the MTZ. These

penetration beneath the CVF, as follows:

Response: We should emphasize that the teleseismic tomography method used in our
study is totally different from that illustrated in Chen et al. (2017). The teleseismic
double-difference tomography method adopted in our study uses differential times from
regional events recorded by global seismic stations, instead of travel times from
teleseismic events recorded by regional stations. In addition, we did not use relative
travel time residuals determined by subtracting average delay times in the study region.
Therefore, our teleseismic tomography method will not create artifacts shown in Chen
et al. (2017). Actually, the tomography method used in Tang et al. (2014) is also
different from that in Chen et al. (2017). Tang et al. (2014) used finite-frequency
tomography method, which employs Born-Fréchet kernels to account for effects of off-
raypath structures on traveltime data. The data they used in the inversion are differential
travel times between station pairs which are measured by a cross-correlation based
method. Consequently, both the data processing procedure and the tomography method
used by Tang et al. (2014) are different from those applied by Chen et al. (2017).
Moreover, two independent seismic tomography studies, Tao et al. (2018) and Ma et al.
(2018), also vaguely imaged the local slab penetration into the lower mantle, consistent
with our velocity images. As a consequence, the slab gap or slab tongue for the
subducting Pacific plate is real beneath the CVF. We have made this point clearer in
the Supplementary Materials, as follows:
“For the inversion, we use the multiscale teleseismic double-difference (DD)
tomography method of Pesicek et al. (2014), which is a global version of the DD seismic
tomography method (tomoDD) (Zhang and Thurber, 2003, 2006). It utilizes the pseudo-
bending raytracing algorithm (Um and Thurber, 1987) to determine the ray paths and
compute the travel times between events and stations within a spherical Earth model.
The pseudo-bending raytracing method is very efficient and has been widely used in
seismic tomography studies at various scales (e.g., Zhao et al., 1992; Chiarabba et al.,
2000; Rawlingson et al., 2010).
Compared to the conventional teleseismic tomography method, as described in Chen et
al. (2017), the teleseismic DD tomography method uses both absolute event-station
arrival times and differential arrival times from pairs of regional events observed on
global seismic stations to simultaneously determine event locations and seismic velocity
models. This is in contrast to the conventional teleseismic tomography method that uses
arrival times from teleseismic events recorded on regional seismic stations to determine
velocity structure beneath stations. As a result, teleseismic DD tomography method is
not subject to potential artifacts introduced by conventional teleseismic tomography
described in Chen et al. (2017).”
